title: One Hundred Fifty Years of Land Values in Chicago: A Nonparametric Approach (McMillen, Journal of Urban Economics 40(1): 100-124, July 1996)
what_was_fetched: ABSTRACT ONLY. (1) One ordinary request to the DOI: HTTP 200 after redirect to a linkinghub.elsevier.com stub page (meta-refresh to ScienceDirect); no text served, not followed further (item1-doi-response.txt). (2) IDEAS/RePEc record: bibliographic only, 'No abstract is available', 'Full text for ScienceDirect subscribers only', 155 citations listed (item1-ideas-repec.txt/.html). (3) Illinois Experts portal record: full abstract served as plain HTML (item1-illinois-experts.txt/.html). Web search found no working-paper or repository PDF and no McMillen-hosted copy. Full text is NOT open; no data, figures, tables or page locators inside the paper are available.
verdict: ENRICH research/hoyt-chicago-land-values.md from the abstract (NOT a new page). Also add a BACKLOG [LEAD] tier:T1 for the full text (publisher-only; look for a Chicago Fed or UIC working-paper version). Anchor sentence (Nuances and Limits, first bullet, exact text): "Hoyt's data and methods reflect 1930s social-science practice: descriptive statistics, maps, and narrative synthesis rather than the regression-based causal-inference methods used in modern urban and public economics." Suggested addition after that bullet: one sentence that McMillen (1996, Journal of Urban Economics 40(1): 100-124) later fitted locally weighted (nonparametric) regressions to Chicago land values for 1836-1990, finding that a monocentric land-value surface fits 1836-1928 only if the functional form is highly nonlinear and that by 1960-1990 Chicago is no longer monocentric (O'Hare Airport an employment centre; blighted south and west sides below the model's prediction). Cite as Tier 1 peer-reviewed; access phrased impersonally in Sources only (abstract-based).
claim_grade: A for the existence and bibliographic facts; B for the method/finding statements (peer-reviewed article by a recognised urban economist, Tier 1 per EDITORIAL 4c; McMillen is not in people-tiers.json, academic default = Tier 1) but graded from the abstract only. Nothing quantitative can be carried.
content_summary: Abstract (Illinois Experts, verbatim in substance): 'Locally weighted regression estimates are presented for Chicago using data from 1836 to 1990. The results demonstrate that nonparametric estimators are useful for hypothesis testing as well as prediction. Estimated regression surfaces for 1836-1928 demonstrate that the monocentric city model continues to adequately represent land values through the early 19th century [sic in portal text; evidently 20th], but only if the functional form is highly nonlinear. Estimates for 1960-1990 indicate that Chicago is no longer a monocentric city; O'Hare Airport is an important employment center and the blighted areas of the south and west sides have lower land values than the model predicts.' Pages 100-124 (25 pp). No figure locators available. NOT verified, because the full text is closed: the data sources (Hoyt 1933 extended with Olcott's Land Values Blue Book to 1986-1990), the number or dates of land-value cycles, and the evolution of the price-distance gradient.
existing_wiki_coverage: research/hoyt-chicago-land-values (Hoyt 1933 page; Nuances bullet above carries the 'pre-modern-econometrics' limitation; no McMillen mention, no 1986-1990 extension, no Olcott), places/chicago (Hoyt as founding source for boom-bust premise; mentions TIF since 1986 only), people/homer-hoyt (cites Harrison on 1990 downturn), concepts/sector-model, research/progress-18-6-year-cycle, narratives/this-time-is-different. No McMillen scholar page. Only McMillen trace anywhere: Thorsnes & McMillen 1998 (parcel size) rejected, BACKLOG line 93 and LOOPLOG 5692 - a different paper.
uncertainties: SCANNER PREMISES THAT FAIL OR ARE UNVERIFIED: (a) 'extends Hoyt's 1933 study 50 further years' / 'echo of Hoyt': the abstract never mentions Hoyt, Olcott, Land Values Blue Book, land-value cycles, boom-bust, or a price-distance gradient; it is about monocentric versus polycentric structure and nonparametric methods. Treat as unconfirmed until the full text is read. (b) 'empirically documents land-value cycles' is NOT in the abstract; do NOT put cycle dates or 'cycles' wording in the wiki on this basis, and it must not be used to support the 18-year-cycle claim. (c) Data span in the abstract is 1836-1990, not '1836-1986'. (d) the 2026-10-26 date is a portal date (scanner correct on that). (e) The portal abstract's 'early 19th century' is almost certainly a typo for 20th; do not quote it. The enrichment is therefore modest (method/structure finding), not the 'quantitative sequel' the scanner suggested; a NEW research page is not justified without full text. Elsevier did not strictly refuse (200 + meta-refresh stub); no further attempt made.

content_summary: COLEMAN-GRIMES (open, read): Motu WP 09-14, 'Fiscal, Distributional and Efficiency Impacts of Land and Property Taxes', September 2009, uses Quotable Value rateable valuations and Statistics NZ SoFIE data. Table 7 area-unit and TLA regressions: 'the coefficient on lnHHY in the land value and capital value equations is significantly greater than unity (using a 95% confidence interval) indicating that both taxes are progressive. The lnHHY coefficient is materially higher for the land value equation than for the capital value equation; consequently a land tax is more progressive (for households) than is a property tax' (printed p. 36 = PDF p. 42). Caveat sentence: 'A land appears to be more progressive than a property tax; however overall progressivity would depend crucially on the nature of other offsetting taxation changes' (printed p. 45 = PDF p. 51). Also: the approach 'cannot attribute causality'; it is a cross-sectional association at area level, and a national land/property tax scenario, not a study of council rating. Scanner wording 'land-based rating is more likely progressive across NZ households' is a fair paraphrase but the paper says more progressive than capital value, and both progressive in the elasticity sense. COUNCIL (official, 13 Nov hub): commercial pays 3.7 times the residential general rate ('$3.70 ... for every $1'), commercial pays 49 percent of the rates pie; proposal to reduce the differential 3.7:1 to 3.0:1 over six years; consultation closes 15 November; oral hearings; decision in December (Committee/Council meeting); 'No decisions have been made yet.' Hub also carries a 13 November service-disruption notice (Microsoft outage; late emailed submissions will be accepted if needed). Matches the wiki page's figures. OP-ED claims (1), (3), (4) beyond the council's own figures and the pass-through to tenants and jobs are UNVERIFIED from the text (the council itself says it 'remains uncertain' whether landlords pass on a cut); point (3) windfall gains returning to the funder not checked against any source.
existing_wiki_coverage: events/2026-wellington-rating-policies-review.md already carries the consultation in full: 3.7:1 to 3.0:1 over six years, 51:49 split, 5.8 differential note, 60%/80% modelling, timeline (December decision), Council doubt about pass-through; no Lees, Donovan, Coleman or Post mention and no incidence/progressivity discussion (its Georgist section only covers efficiency). places/new-zealand.md covers the Wellington proposal in 'Current Debate' (source 16) and Gemmell-Grimes-Skidmore; no Coleman-Grimes 2009; Grimes appears only as co-author of GGS and McCluskey-Grimes-Timmins. Digest grep for Coleman, Motu, Lees, Donovan: no people/research pages. Possible new research page for Coleman & Grimes 2009 (open full text, Tier 1) is better value than the op-ed: suggest NEW research/coleman-grimes-land-property-taxes as an optional follow-up.
uncertainties: (1) Op-ed text, headline, standfirst, byline not seen; all attributions (affiliations 'Senior Fellow, Motu', 'Lees Economic Consulting / University of Canterbury research fellow') come from the scanner. Scanner premise 'full text fetched' holds only for the scanner, not here. (2) The scanner says the authors cite Coleman and Grimes; which paper they cite is unknown. If the op-ed cites a different or newer paper, the anchor should be redone. (3) The 2009 paper is old; no newer Motu paper checked. (4) Consultation outcome: none yet. As of 13 Nov the hub says no decisions, closes 15 Nov, decision in December; wellington.govt.nz refused one request (403). Re-check after the December committee meeting. (5) The Motu page had Donovan's bio; no 'Senior Fellow' label seen. Do not include any email addresses (page lists none used).

title: Pinning the Wage to Scarcity and Technology (Johan Bage and Stella Wilson; SSRN 7226858, 39 pp, 23 Sep 2026 version)
what_was_fetched: SSRN: one ordinary request, HTTP 403 Cloudflare 'Just a moment' challenge (item3-ssrn-response.txt); stopped. Authors' own public repository github.com/wilsoniumite/labor cloned shallow via the session git proxy (dl3/labor, 807 MB): pinning/paper/ssrn-7226858.pdf is the SSRN-posted 23 Sep 2026 PDF (copied to dl3/ssrn-7226858.pdf; 39 pages; text item3-ssrn-7226858-fulltext.txt) READ IN FULL IN SUBSTANCE (abstract, intro, Secs 2-9, 11, AI-use note, data note; appendices skimmed). Also read pinning/README.md, STATE.md, lean/README.md, effort/code/build_fig3_realwage_fork_1950.py. Independent check: downloaded the three FRED series (item3-fred-AHETPI-CUSR0000SAD-SAH1.txt; dl1/fred.csv, public FRED CSV endpoint, one request).
verdict: DEFER: add a BACKLOG [LEAD] tier:T3 (unrefereed preprint; re-check on journal acceptance) and make no wiki page now; do not cite the paper as support anywhere. The 4.8x figure, if wanted, can be cited directly to BLS series via FRED (and is better attributed to the data than to the paper), but no wiki page currently has a hook for it. REJECT as a NEW page. If the editor wants a citable fact: a one-line origin-only mention in concepts/citizens-dividend is the most it could carry, stated as the authors' model result, with no empirical weight. No anchor sentence given because no ENRICH/NEW is recommended.
claim_grade: D as support for any claim about automation, wages or rents (theoretical model, no refereeing; the authors disclose AI-drafted formalisation, proofs, computations, figures and some prose). Tier 3 under 4c (unknown authors, AI-writing disclosure, zero citations as claimed; origin-only at best). The underlying BLS/FRED data points are A/B on their own, independent of the paper. Both authors are unknown to the wiki (not in people-tiers.json): Johan Bage listed at Stockholm School of Economics; Stella Wilson at KTH Royal Institute of Technology and SEB (a bank), per the title-page footnotes, plus a disclaimer that views are their own.
content_summary: MODEL: task-assignment (Acemoglu-Restrepo margin) plus a production network (Leontief/Sraffa cost system). At the interior task margin the wage equals the cost of the machine substitute (Prop 1); replacement closure (Prop 2, eq. 5) shows two automation channels, lower relative human productivity at the margin and less labour embodied in machine production, both lowering w/r. CENTRAL OBJECT: the wage-rent ratio (w/r; the appendix normalises r = 1 and writes v = w/r, p. 28, Appendix B). BOUNDS (Prop 4, eq. 12): w/p_i = 1/(lambda_i + b_i(r/w)); embodied rent requirement caps wage purchasing power, a feasible human method gives a lower bound; if w/r tends to 0 and b_i stays bounded away from 0, purchasing power tends to 0. PARTICIPATION (Props 3 and 5 sections): outside option priced by the same network. LABOUR SHARE (Prop 5, eq. 15, p. 15): share = (w/r)Na / ((w/r)Na + T); with bounded hours and fixed T, w/r to 0 sends labour's share to 0. POLICY (Sec 7, Prop 6, pp. 15-17): a tax on pure rents at rate tau_R funds a uniform per-person transfer d = tau_R R/N, paid in and out of work; fixed-factor supply invariant to the tax; coverage kappa = R/(N Ps); tax rate 1/kappa funds one basket. Measured kappa = 0.33 [0.18-0.59] in 2025, up from about 0.05 in the 1950s (Fig 6, p. 20); 0.68 of tax revenue from labour-income bases (Sec 11, p. 22). FORK (Sec 9, p. 19; Fig 5, p. 20): average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers deflated by CPI durables versus CPI shelter, ratio 4.8x over 1964-2024; food-deflated wage +13 percent, durables +277 percent, shelter -21 percent. DATA TRACE: repo script uses FRED/BLS AHETPI (wage), CUSR0000SAD (CPI durables), CUSR0000SAH1 (CPI shelter), spliced backward for the 1950-63 extension only. INDEPENDENT REPRODUCTION from the FRED CSV (annual means, 1964 vs 2024): durables-deflated wage 3.77x, shelter-deflated 0.79x, ratio 4.79 = 4.8x; matches the paper. It is a descriptive ratio the authors themselves say 'requires additional task-level evidence' to attribute. Shelter CPI includes owner-equivalent rent, so it is a proxy, not land rent. Financing versus production (Fig 7, p. 21): labour-origin finance 69.6 percent of consumption in 2004 and 65.8 percent in 2023 versus human effort 48.9 and 47.2 percent of consumed production. AI SECTION (Sec 11, p. 22): AI can lower both margins; scarcities named: sites, water, minerals, grid access, legal rights. GEORGE: cited as 'the fiscal lineage' (George 1879; Arnott-Stiglitz theorem 'related but distinct'), Ricardo/Malthus wage-subsistence in Sec 2.5. AI DISCLOSURE (p. 37, verbatim in substance): 'written in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI). The theory and its central claims are the authors'; parts of the formalization, proofs, computations, figures, and some initial prose were drafted by Claude Fable 5 and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol under the authors' direction and review. All data were pulled live from public sources; the code and data are public. Errors remain the authors'.' LEAN: pinning/lean builds with 0 errors, 0 sorry, 119 declarations (66 corner spine, 53 pinning extension), Lean 4.33.0 and mathlib v4.33.0; this is the authors' own README claim, not re-built here. STATUS: the repo's STATE.md says a version was prepared for an Economic Modelling special issue (AI, Data Investment and the Digital economy), i.e. submitted or about to be, not accepted. Repository history: restructured 2026-09-04.
existing_wiki_coverage: No automation or wage-rent page. Nearest: concepts/citizens-dividend (71 digest entries; rent-funded dividend, Alaska), concepts/margin-of-production (Ricardo/George wage-rent), concepts/wages-fund-doctrine, concepts/stationary-state, research/korinek-stiglitz-ai-rents, research/korinek-lockwood-ai-public-finance (Tier 1 'unexpectedly Georgist' tax design for AI rents), research/leduc-liu-automation-bargaining, research/imf-gen-ai-future-of-work, research/carney-future-of-work, research/openai-industrial-policy-intelligence-age, research/barkai-declining-shares, research/autor-superstar-firms, research/giovannoni-labor-share-decomposition, concepts/superstar-firms, research/kerspien-madsen-strulik-buildings-labor-share. Grep of the digest for 'wage-rent', 'Acemoglu', 'Restrepo', 'Zeira' found nothing; ATCOR is covered at concepts/atcor and research/gaffney-atcor.
uncertainties: Scanner premises all check out: authors and affiliations as stated; 4.8x over 1964-2024 is in the abstract and Sec 9; AI disclosure present (it names Claude and ChatGPT, with specific model names); code, data and Lean public in the repository; 39 pp. Corrections to the scanner: (a) the paper uses w/r in the main text, with v = w/r defined in Appendix B (p. 28); (b) the paper's statements that automation compresses w/r are conditional model results (limits as w/r tends to 0), not an empirical finding that it has happened; the labour-share 'result' is an identity-based limit, and the authors' last section calls the broader implication a 'conjecture ... not establish[ed]'; (c) 'zero citations' not re-verified. (d) Whether the SSRN revision on 23 Sep equals this PDF: the repo README says so; the SSRN page itself was blocked. (e) The repo has a later main.tex (rebuilt 2 Nov, revised for Economic Modelling), so the preprint may change. (f) The Zenodo sibling deposit (10.5281/zenodo.23341696) was not fetched. (g) author email addresses appear on the PDF title page and were not used. (h) Do not assume a Georgist reading: the paper treats the rent tax as a pure redistribution device and cites George for lineage, not as an endorsement of land-value taxation as such; coverage kappa 0.33 means full rent capture funds only a third of a subsistence basket on the authors' own estimate. Re-assess when peer-reviewed.
